benchmark_details.name: Book Advert XML Repair
benchmark_details.overview: Evaluates models on repairing malformed XML markup in transcribed adverts from the Basler Avisblatt (1729–1844), most of them book sale listings tagged for title, author, format and price, while leaving the advert text unchanged.

purpose_and_intended_users.goal: Measure how well language models repair broken XML markup in historical text without altering the text: closing unclosed elements, correcting mismatched tag names and restoring malformed tags, as needed when cleaning the output of automatic tagging pipelines. The results are meant for AI researchers and model developers comparing models on structured-text repair, and for practitioners in digital humanities and editing who post-process semi-structured historical text and choose a model for markup repair.
tasks: preservation of the transcribed text while editing markup
purpose_and_intended_users.limitations:
50 adverts from one newspaper and one tagging scheme. The reference makes one repair where a malformation allows several; the scorer accepts two alternatives (see Calculation): which tag of a mismatched `PRIZE`/`PRICE` pair is renamed, and where in the plain text after an element a closing tag is placed. Every other choice, such as where an unclosed `TITLE` ends or which tags to add, is scored against the reference only, and the prompt's invitation to add tags "where it makes sense" costs precision whenever the reference adds none.

The data keeps two features of the source as real-world noise. 49 of 50 texts carry the same encoding damage (UTF-8 read as Mac Roman, e.g. `B√ºcher` for "Bücher"); the scorer repairs it on both sides, so a model that also repairs it neither gains nor loses. Prices are tagged `PRIZE` in most adverts and `PRICE` in some; consistent pairs stay as they are.
out_of_scope_uses: evaluating XML validation against a schema or DTD
evaluating OCR correction or encoding repair
evaluating tagging of untagged text from scratch

data.source: Adverts from the Basler Avisblatt, the weekly advertising paper of Basel (1729–1844), digitised and processed by the SNSF project "Printed markets: information, data, and news in the Basel 'Avisblatt', 1729–1844" at the University of Basel: https://avisblatt.philhist.unibas.ch/. Most adverts announce books for sale or subscription by booksellers, printers and bookbinders; a few offer other goods. Each is tagged with elements for its bibliographic parts and made malformed.
data.annotation: The repaired ground truth was drafted by a language model and reviewed by the annotator, Sorin Marti, with Ina Serif as domain expert (see Contributors by Role). For version 2.0.0 it was curated to the input text plus markup repairs: text the draft had deleted or changed was restored (a French title block in `line_14`, `à` before prices, commas, OCR corrections such as `Parabieses` to `Paradieses`); renames of already consistent `PRIZE` pairs to `PRICE` were undone; unescaped `&` became `&`; six unclosed `BIBL` elements were closed after their last child and five stray `</TITLE>` in `line_49` removed. The draft's `number_of_fixes` and `explanation` were dropped. The source of the malformations (the project's tagging pipeline or deliberate corruption) is not documented.
data.collection_date: Source documents: the Avisblatt appeared 1729–1844; the years named in the 50 adverts run up to 1748. Added to the benchmark: December 2025.
data.contamination_controls: None. The texts, prompt and ground truth have been public in this repository since December 2025.

methods: zero-shot repair of one advert per request: the prompt [`prompt.txt`](prompts/prompt.txt) with the advert's JSON file attached; new tests use [`prompt_v2.txt`](prompts/prompt_v2.txt), which names the schema's keys

structured JSON output requested with the `CorrectedAdvert` dataclass in all tests but one, which requests no schema; `prompt.txt` names the count key `number_of_fixes`, the schema `number_of_corrections`, and neither is scored
output capped at the repository default of 16,384 tokens per request, adjusted per model in `scripts/benchmark_base.py`
metrics: Edit F1, mean over adverts (`f1_macro`, used for ranking)
Edit F1 over pooled edits (`f1_micro`), with `micro_precision` and `micro_recall`
methodology.calculation: The input `xml_string`, the reference `fixed_xml` and the response's `fixed_xml` are normalised alike: all whitespace removed, UTF-8 read as Mac Roman repaired, and every closing tag that follows plain text which itself follows a closing tag moved up to that closing tag. The strings are split into tokens (whole tags, character references such as `&`, single characters) and diffed against the input with Python's `difflib`. Each deleted, inserted or substituted token at an input position is one edit; renaming either tag of a mismatched `PRIZE`/`PRICE` pair to match the other is one edit, whichever tag is renamed. The advert score is the F1 of the edits shared by response and reference (precision over the response's edits, recall over the reference's). A response without a string `fixed_xml`, or that cannot be parsed, makes no edits and scores 0. `f1_macro` is the mean advert score; `f1_micro` pools the edit counts.
methodology.interpretation: Scores range from 0 to 1; higher is better. 1 means the response makes exactly the reference's repairs and nothing else; returning the input unchanged scores 0. Low precision means edits the reference does not make: changed or dropped text, added or renamed tags. Low recall means missed repairs. A changed character counts as much as a changed tag, so `f1_micro` is dominated by the few responses that rewrite or drop whole adverts; rank by `f1_macro`. A score does not show that the response is well-formed XML.
methodology.baseline_results:
Model results are on the [benchmark page](https://rise-services.rise.unibas.ch/benchmarks/p/benchmarks/book_advert_xml) and in `results/<date>/<test_id>/` at the repository root. Compare runs with the same prompt, scoring rules and ground-truth revision. No fixed model baseline is defined. Copying each input `xml_string` unchanged into `fixed_xml` scores 0. Across the latest run of each of the 100 non-legacy tests, `f1_macro` has a median of 0.27 and a best of 0.61 (claude-fable-5-1).

Observed across models: most answers make the reference's repairs only in part and add edits of their own, such as further tags or corrected spellings; the median test makes exactly the reference's repairs in about 4% of adverts that need them. The task combines syntactic repair, structural reconstruction (adding missing tags) and implicit interpretation (deciding what should be tagged); separate variants for repair only and for enrichment would allow more controlled comparisons.
methodology.validation: The model-drafted ground truth was reviewed by Sorin Marti and curated for version 2.0.0 (see Annotation): every reference keeps its input's text apart from repaired malformed tags, and all 50 parse with `xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring`. Scoring is deterministic; the scorer is covered by `tests/test_book_advert_xml_scoring.py`, including a check that every reference scores 1 against itself.

ethical_and_legal_considerations.privacy_and_anonymity: The adverts name 18th-century booksellers, printers and authors; all are long dead. No living persons are concerned.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.data_licensing: Source material: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Ground truth, prompts and other data created for this benchmark: CC BY 4.0.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.compliance_with_regulations: The advert texts come from the Avisblatt project's published data (Avisdata, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8278751), used under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the licence in that dataset's rights field (its notes say CC BY-SA 4.0). The adverts were printed in the 18th century and the persons named are long dead, so data protection law does not apply. No ethical review was carried out.
